pamphlet_excerpts: States Firstchess: States, the firstchess championship match washeld in 1845.
Internationalchess Tournamentwas: The first internationalchess tournamentwas held in London in 1851.
Painting Circa Edward: This painting (circa 1865) by Edward Harrison May depicts Lady Howe as she checkmates Benjamin Franklin.
Benjamin Franklin Playing: By the 1730s, Benjamin Franklin was playing chess.
step_by_step_procedure: Wasamong Earliest Players: He wasamong the earliest players in the colonies that would becomethe United States.
Franklin His Knowledge: Franklin was able to use his knowledge ofchess to help his diplomatic efforts in England.
Modernchess Tournaments Grew: Modernchess tournaments grew out of these early events, and nationalchess organizations formed, with England and the United Statesleading.
World Chess Organization: In 1924, the world chess organization called FIDE (Fédération Internationale des Échecs) was formed.

pamphlet_excerpts: Learn Appreciate Experiences: Learn to appreciate all of your experiences and what youget from the game.
Several Specific Ways: In several specific ways, chess helps youthink better.
Focuson Moves Opponent: You must focuson your moves and your opponent’s moves to avoid makingmajor mistakes.
Chess Builds Critical: Chess builds critical thinking and problem-solving skills.
step_by_step_procedure: Game Require Decide: Every game will require you to decide whether certain moveswill be better for your position, or not better, or actually worse.
Wrong Move Costyou: A wrong move may costyou one of your pieces or even the game.
Analyze Orcompare Risks: You must analyze orcompare the risks and make the best decision you can.
Creativity Somethingthat: You might have to use your creativity and try somethingthat you think might work, perhaps a play you have never triedbefore.

pamphlet_excerpts: White Player Thewhite: White (the player with thewhite pieces) always moves first, by moving one piece to adifferent square, following the rules of movement for that piece.
Moving Piece Square: By moving a piece to a square that contains a piece belongingto the opponent, a player captures (takes) that piece.
Opponent Piece Then: The opponent’s piece is then removed from the board, and it is out ofplay for the rest of the game.
Requirement Teach Someone: For requirement 3, you will need to teach someone elsehow to play chess.
step_by_step_procedure: Teach Mind Youhave: As you teach, keep in mind what youhave learned and what has been helpful to you.
Essential Thing Chess: The essential thing that makes chess a fascinating gameis the existence of several kinds of pieces that havedifferent moves.
Here Ways Game: Here are the ways a game of chess can end in a draw (deadlocked or tied).
Game Automatically Draw: The game is automatically a draw ifthe player whose turn it is to move is not incheck but has no legal move.

Openings Begin Open: The openings which begin 1. e4 e5 are called open games andare known for aggressive attacking play and frequent combinations.
Openings Begin Closed: The openings which begin 1. d4 d5 are called closed games and areknown for more subtle positional play and less aggressive maneuvering.
Games White Begins: Games in which White begins with 1. e4 and Black replieswith a move other than 1. . e5 are called semi-open games.
step_by_step_procedure: Theyare Unbalanced Exciting: Theyare known for unbalanced and exciting play, often with the twoplayers attacking in different sectors of the board.
Experiment Different: Experiment with many different openings and find ones whichyou are most comfortable playing.
Possible Lose Win: It is possible to lose (or win) a game of chess in only two or fourmoves.
Common Types Quick: The most common types of quick checkmates (whichoften happen to beginners because they ignore the “openingprinciples”) are the fool’s mate.

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain four of the following elements of chess strategy: exploiting weaknesses, force, king safety, pawn structure, space, tempo, and clock management. (b) Explain any five of these chess tactics: clearance sacrifice, decoy, discovered attack, double check, double attack, fork, interposing, overloading, overprotecting, pin, skewer, remove the defender, zwischenzug, and zugzwang. (c) Set up a chessboard as follows and with White to move first, demonstrate how to force checkmate on the Black king: (1) White king on e1, the White rooks on a1 and h1, and the Black king on e5 (2) White king on e1, White queen on d1, Black king on e5 (3) White king on e1, White rook on a1, Black king on e5 (d) With White king on d4, White pawn on e3, and Black king on e6: (1) With White to move, demonstrate how White can force Black to allow their pawn to reach the last rank and be promoted to a queen. (2) With Black to move, demonstrate how Black can force a draw. (e) Set up and solve five direct-mate problems provided by your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Discovered Check Threaten: A discovered check can threaten all the squares in a triangle next to the king in a single move.
King Move Away: The king may be able to move away, or forcing the kingto move to another square could create an opportunity todeliver checkmate.
Move Seems Work: When no other move seems to work, the composerof the chess problem may have implied a move, likecastling or an en passant pawn capture.
King Androok Their: If the king androok are on their original squares, assume they havenot moved and castling is possible.
step_by_step_procedure: Pawns Positioned Adjacent: If pawns are positioned on adjacent files in row four or five, assume the first move could be to capture a pawn en passant.
Situation Shown White: In the situation shown, White is to checkmate in onemove and all the squares that need to be attacked are on the first row.
White King Cannot: Also, the white king cannot move to the second rowbecause of the black rook at c2.
White Castling Kingside: White castling kingside is theonly possible solution to this problem.

step_by_step_procedure: Chess Clocks Control: Chess clocks are used to control the length of chess games bylimiting the time allowed for a given number of moves or thecomplete game.

Player Time Runs: If a player’s time runs out, that player loses the game.
